definition:
The Bible's teaching on government holds two truths in tension, and the whole Christian tradition of political thought is an attempt to keep both. The first is that civil authority is a gift of God's providence. Rulers are to restrain evil and do justice, and Paul can call the Roman magistrate “God's servant for your good” (Romans 13:4). Christians therefore owe the state honor, taxes, prayer, and obedience within its proper limits. The second is that rulers are creatures under God, and when they claim what belongs to God they become something monstrous. Daniel sees the empires of the world as beasts rising from the sea (Daniel 7), and Revelation 13 portrays imperial power, backed by the dragon, demanding worship and waging war on the saints. Between these poles stands Israel's own experience of kings judged by the law and confronted by prophets. Over all of it stands the church's oldest confession, that “Jesus Christ is Lord” (Philippians 2:11), which in the Roman world was a claim Caesar also made for himself. Christians have disagreed about how church and state should relate, but every tradition has had to reckon with that confession. This study traces the biblical witness; the site's page on church and state surveys the major Christian views at length, and the study of the kingdom of God treats God's reign itself.

The Hebrew vocabulary is the vocabulary of rule and judgment. Melek is king; shofet, a judge, is one who restores right order, which is why the book of Judges is named for deliverers. The paired words mishpat, justice or right judgment, and tsedaqah, righteousness, describe what a ruler owes, especially to the weak (Psalm 72:1-2). Saul is first designated nagid, a leader or prince appointed by God (1 Samuel 9:16; 10:1), and David after him (1 Samuel 13:14). In the New Testament, exousia means authority or rightful power, and Paul's “governing authorities” in Romans 13:1 are exousiai, a word he also uses of spiritual powers elsewhere (Colossians 2:15); interpreters debate whether Romans 13 has both in view, though most read it of human officials. Paul calls the ruler a diakonos, a servant (Romans 13:4), and officials leitourgoi, public servants (Romans 13:6), a word that in the Greek world named those who performed public service and in Scripture often names ministers of worship. Kyrios, ‘lord’, was used of the emperor, and Kaisar is simply ‘Caesar’. Paul says the church's politeuma, its citizenship or commonwealth, is in heaven (Philippians 3:20), and Peter calls believers “foreigners and exiles” (1 Peter 2:11).
ot:
Genesis grounds human authority over life and death in the image of God: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed; for in His own image God has made mankind” (Genesis 9:6). Many interpreters, from the Reformers onward, have seen here the root of civil justice, a delegated responsibility to restrain violence. Genesis also shows a believer serving a pagan state well: Joseph governs Egypt's grain and saves many lives (Genesis 41:39-57). Exodus shows the same state turned predator. A new Pharaoh enslaves Israel and orders Hebrew boys killed, and the first act of civil disobedience in Scripture follows: the midwives Shiphrah and Puah “feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed” (Exodus 1:17). God's deliverance of Israel is a judgment on a state that made itself a god.

At Sinai Israel receives a law that places every authority under God. Moses appoints judges who are “God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain” (Exodus 18:21) and charges them, “Show no partiality in judging” because “judgment belongs to God” (Deuteronomy 1:17). Deuteronomy commands, “Pursue justice, and justice alone” (Deuteronomy 16:20). Its law of the king (Deuteronomy 17:14-20) anticipates monarchy and limits it at once: the king must not multiply horses, wives, or wealth, must write a copy of the law and read it all his life, and must not consider himself above “his countrymen”. The king is under the law, not above it. In the period of the judges Gideon refuses a crown with the words “The LORD shall rule over you” (Judges 8:23), yet the book ends with chaos and the refrain “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). The Bible thus records both the danger of kings and the danger of having none.

When the elders ask Samuel for a king “like all the other nations”, God tells him, “they have rejected Me as their king”, and Samuel warns that the king “will take” their sons, daughters, fields, and harvests (1 Samuel 8:5-18). God grants the request and works through it, choosing David and promising him an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7). But the prophets hold kings to account. Nathan confronts David over Bathsheba and Uriah with the words “You are that man” (2 Samuel 12:7); Elijah confronts Ahab over Naboth's vineyard, “Have you not murdered a man and seized his land?” (1 Kings 21:19). The psalms picture the ideal king as one who will “vindicate the afflicted” and “crush the oppressor” (Psalm 72:4), and Psalm 2 summons the rulers of the earth to “Serve the LORD with fear” and to honor his anointed king. Wisdom says, “By me kings reign, and rulers enact just laws” (Proverbs 8:15), and charges the king to “defend the cause of the poor and needy” (Proverbs 31:9). The prophets pronounce woe on “those who enact unjust statutes” (Isaiah 10:1), and Jeremiah tells a king that doing justice for the poor is what it means to know the LORD (Jeremiah 22:15-16).

The exile teaches Israel to live under foreign powers. God calls Nebuchadnezzar “My servant” (Jeremiah 27:6) and Cyrus “His anointed” (Isaiah 45:1), so that even pagan rulers serve God's purpose, often without knowing it. Jeremiah tells the exiles in Babylon to build, plant, marry, and “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). Daniel and his friends serve Babylon and Persia faithfully but refuse to worship the king's statue or stop praying to their God: “we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up” (Daniel 3:18; compare Daniel 6:10). Nebuchadnezzar is humbled until he learns “that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind” (Daniel 4:17). Daniel 7 then sees the empires as four beasts from the sea, until “One like the Son of Man” receives from the Ancient of Days an everlasting dominion “that will not pass away” (Daniel 7:13-14). Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther show God's people finding favor and doing good within a Persian empire they did not rule. The Old Testament ends with no Israelite king on the throne and a hope set on the kingdom of God.
nt:
Jesus was born under “a decree” of “Caesar Augustus” (Luke 2:1) and crucified by a Roman governor on a charge of claiming to be king. In the wilderness the devil offers him “all the kingdoms of the world” in exchange for worship, and he refuses (Luke 4:5-8). He calls Herod Antipas “that fox” (Luke 13:32), and he contrasts the rulers of the nations, who “lord it over them” and call themselves benefactors, with his own way: “the one who leads like the one who serves” (Luke 22:25-26). When his opponents try to trap him with a question about the imperial tax, he asks whose image is on the coin and answers, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's” (Mark 12:17). The saying gives Caesar a real due and sets a limit to it, since what bears God's image, the human person, belongs to God. Before Pilate he says, “My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight” (John 18:36), and he tells Pilate that his authority to crucify was “given to you from above” (John 19:11). The chief priests' cry, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15), is the Gospel's picture of religious leaders surrendering to the state what belongs to God. After the resurrection Jesus claims, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me” (Matthew 28:18).

In Acts the apostles respect Roman order and use its protections, yet obey God first. Ordered to stop preaching, Peter and the apostles answer, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Paul insists on his rights as a Roman citizen after an illegal beating in Philippi (Acts 16:37) and appeals to Caesar for a fair trial (Acts 25:11), while his opponents accuse the believers of “saying that there is another king, named Jesus” (Acts 17:7). Paul's fullest teaching comes in Romans 13:1-7, written under Nero. Every person is to submit to the governing authorities, since “there is no authority except that which is from God”; the ruler “does not carry the sword in vain” and is “God's servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer”; therefore Christians pay taxes and give “respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due”. The passage follows directly on Romans 12's command not to avenge oneself but to overcome evil with good, which suggests that the state's restraint of evil is one way God's wrath works in the present age, so that believers need not take vengeance themselves. Paul also tells Timothy to pray “for kings and all those in authority” so that believers may lead “tranquil and quiet lives” (1 Timothy 2:2), and Titus to remind believers “to submit to rulers and authorities” (Titus 3:1).

Peter writes to scattered churches facing slander and suffering. He calls them “a royal priesthood, a holy nation” and “foreigners and exiles” (1 Peter 2:9, 11), tells them to submit “for the Lord's sake to every human institution”, and ends with a carefully ordered line: “Love the brotherhood of believers, fear God, honor the king” (1 Peter 2:13, 17). The king is honored, like everyone; only God is feared. Paul, too, tells the Philippians, who lived in a Roman colony proud of its citizenship, that “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20), and celebrates the day when “every tongue” will “confess that Jesus Christ is Lord” (Philippians 2:11). The risen Christ is seated “far above all rule and authority, power and dominion” (Ephesians 1:21), and on the cross he has already “disarmed the powers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15).

Revelation shows the other face of the state. In chapter 13 a beast rises from the sea, receives from the dragon “his power and his throne and great authority”, is worshiped by the world, and makes war on the saints; a second beast enforces worship of its image and controls who may “buy or sell” (Revelation 13:2-17). Most interpreters see Rome's imperial cult in the background, though they differ on how much the vision also describes later powers or the end of history. In chapters 17 and 18 Babylon, the great city, grows rich on luxury and trade and is drunk with the blood of the saints, and she falls. Yet the book's last word on rulers is not only judgment. The seventh trumpet announces that “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ” (Revelation 11:15), the rider on the white horse bears the name “KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS” (Revelation 19:16), and the kings of the earth bring their glory into the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:24). Romans 13 and Revelation 13 belong to the same canon. The state is God's servant when it does justice and a beast when it demands worship, and discernment between the two is part of Christian faithfulness.

keyTexts.why: God requires an accounting for human blood because humanity bears his image, which many have read as the root of civil justice.
The midwives fear God rather than Pharaoh and refuse his command to kill, the Bible's first account of faithful civil disobedience.
The law of the king limits royal power and places the king under God's written law, beside his countrymen, not above them.
Israel demands a king like the nations, God names it a rejection of his own rule, and Samuel warns of everything a king will take.
Elijah confronts Ahab over Naboth's murder, showing the prophet holding the powerful to account under God's law.
The prayer for the king defines good rule as justice for the afflicted and the needy and the crushing of the oppressor.
Exiles are told to seek the prosperity of Babylon and pray for it, a model for God's people living under foreign power.
Three servants of the Babylonian state refuse to worship the king's image whatever the cost, drawing the line obedience may not cross.
The empires appear as beasts, and dominion is given to one like the Son of Man, whose kingdom will never be destroyed.
Jesus gives Caesar his due and God his, granting the state real claims and limiting them at the same stroke.
Jesus tells Pilate that his authority is given from above, and the chief priests declare they have no king but Caesar.
When authorities forbid the gospel, the apostles answer that they must obey God rather than men.
The central New Testament text: governing authorities are appointed by God to restrain evil, and Christians owe them submission, taxes, respect, and honor.
Exiles submit to every human institution for the Lord's sake and honor the king, while fearing God alone.
The state absolutized becomes a beast empowered by the dragon, demanding worship and making war on the saints, the counterweight to Romans 13.

history:
For its first three centuries the church lived as a suspect minority. Christians prayed for the emperor, paid taxes, and insisted they were loyal, yet refused to offer sacrifice or incense to the emperor's image. Pliny the Younger's letter to the emperor Trajan (around 112) describes testing accused Christians in exactly this way, and the account of Polycarp's martyrdom, around the middle of the second century, describes officials urging the aged bishop to say ‘Caesar is Lord’ and offer incense, which he refused. After Constantine's conversion and the agreement of 313 known as the Edict of Milan, persecution ended, and by Theodosius I's edict of 380 Nicene Christianity became the official religion of the empire. The church now had to think about rulers who were Christians. Ambrose of Milan required Theodosius to do public penance after the massacre at Thessalonica in 390, a sign that the emperor stood under the church's moral judgment. Augustine's City of God (413 to 426), written after the sack of Rome, described two cities formed by two loves and refused to identify any empire with the kingdom of God. In the East, Justinian's Sixth Novella (535) described priesthood and empire as two gifts of God meant to work in harmony, the ideal later called symphonia. In the West, Pope Gelasius I's letter to the emperor Anastasius (494) distinguished the sacred authority of bishops from royal power, a distinction that fed centuries of conflict between popes and kings, from the Investiture Controversy and Henry IV's penance at Canossa (1077) to Boniface VIII's bull Unam Sanctam (1302).

The Reformation multiplied the answers. Luther's Temporal Authority: To What Extent It Should Be Obeyed (1523) distinguished God's rule through the gospel from his rule through the sword and denied that rulers could command faith. The Anabaptist Schleitheim Confession (1527) held that the sword is ordained by God but outside the perfection of Christ, so that believers should not serve as magistrates. Calvin's Institutes closed with a chapter on civil government (book 4, chapter 20), honoring the magistrate's calling while allowing that lesser magistrates might restrain a tyrant, a line developed by the Magdeburg Confession (1550) and later by Samuel Rutherford's Lex, Rex (1644). Most Reformation churches still assumed that rulers should uphold true religion, and dissenters of every kind, Anabaptists above all, were imprisoned, exiled, or executed by Catholics and Protestants alike. Against this the Baptist Thomas Helwys, in A Short Declaration of the Mystery of Iniquity (1612), argued that the king has no power over the souls of his subjects, and Roger Williams, who founded Providence in 1636, argued for liberty of conscience for all. The Westminster Confession (1646) gave the magistrate duties toward the church, a chapter American Presbyterians revised in 1788 to remove that power, and the First Amendment to the United States Constitution (1791) forbade a national establishment of religion.

The twentieth century tested every tradition. In Germany the movement of the German Christians sought to fuse the church with National Socialism, and the Confessing Church's Barmen Declaration (May 1934), drafted chiefly by Karl Barth, confessed Jesus Christ as the one Word of God and rejected any other lords or sources of revelation. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, drawn into the resistance, was executed at Flossenbürg in April 1945. Martin Luther King Jr.'s Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963) appealed to Augustine and Aquinas to argue that an unjust law is no true law and may be broken openly and nonviolently. The Second Vatican Council's Declaration on Religious Freedom, Dignitatis Humanae (1965), affirmed religious liberty as a right grounded in human dignity, and South African theologians' Kairos Document (1985) challenged churches that had given theological cover to apartheid. In the same century Christians of the left and the right warned one another against identifying the gospel with their own programs. Reinhold Niebuhr's Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932) criticized the liberal optimism of the Social Gospel, and later critics on the right and left have warned against Christian nationalism and against a church that simply echoes a party.

differ.body: In the Lutheran tradition and in one strand of Reformed thought, God rules the world in two ways: through the gospel and the church, which bring forgiveness and faith, and through law and the civil order, which restrain evil among all people. Both are God's, but they must not be confused. The state need not be Christian to be legitimate; it must be just, and it governs by the moral law known to all. The church does not wield the sword or seek to run the state; it preaches the gospel. Defenders point to Jesus' saying about Caesar's coin, his refusal of the sword (John 18:36), and Paul's description of a pagan magistrate as God's servant (Romans 13:4).

Neo-Calvinists, following Abraham Kuyper, hold that there is no neutral zone in human life, so politics, like every sphere, stands under the lordship of Christ. They teach sphere sovereignty: family, church, school, business, and state each have their own God-given authority and none may swallow the others. Christians therefore work within public life for justice shaped by biblical principles, without seeking a state church. Defenders point to Psalm 2's summons to the kings of the earth, to Christ's authority over all things (Matthew 28:18; Colossians 1:15-20), and to the prophets' concern for just laws, and they cite the long record of Christians who changed unjust laws.

differ.view: The church as a witnessing community
differ.body: The Anabaptist and Mennonite churches, and theologians such as Stanley Hauerwas, hold that the church's first political task is to be the church: a community that lives by the Sermon on the Mount, refuses violence, forgives, and shares its goods, and so shows the world an alternative to its politics of coercion. Christians honor rulers and pray for them but do not seek to govern the world by the sword. Defenders point to Jesus' refusal of the sword, his teaching on loving enemies (Matthew 5:38-48), his contrast between the rulers of the Gentiles and his servant disciples (Luke 22:25-26), and Peter's description of believers as exiles.

Catholic social teaching, building on Augustine and Thomas Aquinas, holds that the state serves the common good, the conditions that allow persons, families, and communities to flourish, and that it should respect subsidiarity, leaving to smaller communities what they can do themselves. Natural law, known by reason, gives believers and unbelievers shared ground for public argument. Since Dignitatis Humanae (1965) the Catholic Church has affirmed religious liberty for all. Defenders point to Jeremiah 29:7, to Romans 13, and to the moral law written on the heart (Romans 2:14-15), and they hold that politics matters greatly but saves no one.

Eastern Orthodox churches have long spoken of a symphonia between church and state, each serving God in its own sphere, and some Protestant nations kept established churches, such as the Church of England. A small number of Reformed thinkers, the theonomists, go further and hold that civil law should follow the moral and judicial law of Moses. Defenders of establishment argue that a society cannot be neutral about ultimate things, that Psalm 2 and Isaiah's picture of kings serving God's people (Isaiah 49:23) envision rulers who honor Christ, and that a public acknowledgment of God can coexist with toleration. Critics within the church answer that establishment has too often bound the church to the state's interests, and most traditions now defend religious liberty.

errors:
The church has rejected any teaching that gives the state what belongs to God. The early Christians died rather than call Caesar lord, and the Barmen Declaration rejected the claim that a nation, a race, or a leader could stand beside Christ as a source of revelation. Christian nationalism in any country, the fusion of Christian faith with a nation's identity so that the nation is treated as God's chosen people, its enemies as God's enemies, and political power as the means of the church's mission, repeats this error. It treats the promises made to Israel and the church as belonging to a modern state, and it turns the cross into a flag. The mirror image of this error is equally real. A progressive Christianity that identifies the kingdom of God with a political program of social reform, treats its party's platform as the gospel's content, and regards its opponents as enemies of God makes the same mistake from the other side. Both reduce the church to a voting bloc, both expect from the state a salvation only Christ gives (Psalm 146:3), and both find it hard to love the neighbor across the political divide. The church's task is to test every political claim, including those of the side it favors, by the same Scripture and with the same humility.

The church has also, though too slowly, repudiated its own past use of state power to coerce belief, the burning and drowning of dissenters by Catholics and Protestants, which Jesus' refusal of the sword condemns. It has rejected the opposite errors too: contempt for all authority, which Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2 forbid, and a quietism that tells believers to obey any command and ignore injustice, which the midwives, Daniel, the apostles, and the prophets refute. Obedience to rulers is real and limited; when rulers command what God forbids or forbid what God commands, Christians must obey God, openly and without violence, and accept the cost.
life:
This doctrine shapes ordinary citizenship. It calls believers to pray for those in authority by name, whether they voted for them or not, to pay taxes, to obey just laws, to speak honestly and respectfully of rulers, and to seek the good of the place where they live, as the exiles in Babylon were told. It frees them from expecting salvation from any election or party, and from despair when their side loses, because the kingdom of God does not rise or fall with a vote. It also calls them to speak for the poor and the voiceless, as Scripture charges kings to do, and to refuse any command that would require them to deny Christ or harm the innocent.

The doctrine also guards the heart. It is easy to love a nation or a cause more than the neighbor, and easy to think of fellow believers on the other side of a political divide as enemies. Peter's order, fear God and honor the king, keeps each loyalty in its place. A Christian can be a grateful citizen and a faithful exile at the same time, holding a passport from an earthly nation and a citizenship in heaven, and looking for the day when the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of Christ.
questions: Romans 13 calls the ruler God's servant, and Revelation 13 portrays a ruler as a beast. What marks the difference between the two, and how can Christians recognize when a government is moving from one toward the other?
The midwives, Daniel, and the apostles disobeyed rulers to obey God, yet Paul and Peter call believers to submit and honor. How do you decide when obedience must give way to conscience?

Christians on the right and on the left have both been tempted to identify the gospel with their own political program. Where are you most tempted to do so, and what would it look like to test your own side by Scripture first?
